result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_laplacian_spectrum()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L29482-L29725){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_laplacian_spectrum( which="smallest", k=None, normalized=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Laplacian spectrum](/assets/graphs/get-laplacian-spectrum.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph, two triangles sharing an edge plus a pendant, and a bar chart of the five eigenvalues of its Laplacian D minus A, sorted from smallest to largest: 0.000, 0.830, 2.689, 4.000, and 4.481. The single zero means the graph is connected, and the second-smallest eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity 0.830, is in the accent color." width="100%"} Returns the spectrum of the Laplacian matrix `L = D - A` (or normalized variant). The Laplacian spectrum provides insights into graph connectivity, cuts, and diffusion processes. `A` is the weighted adjacency matrix used by `get_spectrum()` and `D` is the diagonal matrix of its row sums (out-degrees for directed graphs), matching `networkx.laplacian_matrix()`. Parallel edges sum their weights and self-loops cancel out of `L`, so its rows always sum to zero. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [which]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["smallest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which eigenvalues to return: `"all"` for all `n` eigenvalues, `"smallest"` for the smallest `k`, or `"largest"` for the largest `k`. For directed graphs, "largest" and "smallest" are by real part. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of eigenvalues to return for `"largest"`/`"smallest"`. Default is `min(6, n)` where `n` is the number of nodes. [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, use the normalized Laplacian `L_norm = D^(-1/2) L D^(-1/2)`, where isolated nodes get a zero row and column (as in `networkx.normalized_laplacian_matrix()`). Its eigenvalues lie in `[0, 2]` for undirected graphs. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Dictionary with keys: - `"values"`: list of eigenvalues, sorted ascending - `"vectors"`: list of unit eigenvectors aligned with `"values"`; entry `j` of each vector belongs to node `nodes[j]` - `"nodes"`: node IDs, in creation order, giving the order of eigenvector entries - `"algebraic_connectivity"`: `λ₂` over the full spectrum (second-smallest eigenvalue; `0` if disconnected, `None` for a single node) For directed graphs the Laplacian is not symmetric, so `"values"` holds Python `complex` numbers sorted by real part, and `"vectors"` and `"algebraic_connectivity"` are `None`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is empty, `which` is invalid, or the eigenvalue computation fails to converge. ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - spectral clustering: use Fiedler vector for graph partitioning - community detection: k-way clustering using k eigenvectors - graph cuts: min-cut via spectral relaxation - synchronization: analyze coupled oscillators on networks - diffusion processes: heat kernel and random walks - network robustness: algebraic connectivity as connectivity measure ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The Laplacian $L = D - A$ carries the same structural information as the adjacency matrix but organized so that its algebraic properties align with graph connectivity in particularly clean ways. $L$ is always positive semi-definite, so its spectrum is non-negative, and it *always* has a zero eigenvalue whose eigenvector is the constant vector $\mathbf{1}$. The multiplicity of that zero eigenvalue is exactly the number of connected components, so counting near-zero eigenvalues is the direct spectral test for disconnection. The second-smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_2$, called the *algebraic connectivity* or Fiedler value, is positive iff the graph is connected and quantifies expansion through Cheeger's inequality $\tfrac{h^2}{2\Delta} \le \lambda_2 \le 2h$, where $h$ is edge expansion. Its eigenvector (the *Fiedler vector*) partitions the graph into two well-connected halves by sign, minimizing normalized cut weight in the spectral-relaxation sense, and is the workhorse of spectral bisection algorithms. Passing `normalized=True` switches to $L_{\mathrm{norm}} = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}$, whose eigenvalues sit in $[0, 2]$ regardless of degree distribution; a $\lambda = 2$ eigenvalue signals a bipartite component. This variant is standard in normalized-cut clustering because it handles degree-imbalanced graphs (star-plus-clique structures, for instance) far more gracefully than the plain Laplacian. Signature spectra include $K_n \to \{0, n, \ldots, n\}$, the path $P_n \to \{2 - 2\cos(\pi k / n)\}$, the cycle $C_n \to \{2 - 2\cos(2\pi k / n)\}$, and the star $S_n \to \{0, 1, \ldots, 1, n\}$. For undirected graphs with at least 400 nodes, `"smallest"` and `"largest"` with a small `k` use a sparse block solver (Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration) that scales to very large graphs and resolves repeated eigenvalues, such as the many zero eigenvalues of a disconnected graph. Results match the dense solver to about `1e-11` relative to the spectral radius. Convergence depends on the requested eigenvalues' gap relative to the width of the spectrum. The smallest eigenvalues of the *unnormalized* Laplacian are the hard case on graphs with high-degree hubs, since hub degrees stretch the spectrum: on a 200,000-node Barabási-Albert graph they take minutes, while `normalized=True` takes seconds. `"all"`, small graphs, and directed graphs use a dense $O(n^3)$ eigendecomposition, practical up to a few thousand nodes. ## Examples {.doc-examples} **Detecting Disconnected Components** The number of zero eigenvalues in the Laplacian spectrum equals the number of connected components, so a graph made of two separate pieces has exactly two eigenvalues at (or very near) zero: ::: {#f800bfd9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Graph with 2 components g = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Component 1 g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") # Component 2 g.add_node(label="X") g.add_node(label="Y") g.add_edge(source="X", target="Y") spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=3) # λ₁ = 0 has multiplicity = number of connected components # Returns 2 (the number of components) sum(1 for v in spec['values'] if abs(v) < 1e-6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#01804ff3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Algebraic connectivity (= 0 means disconnected) spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0.0 ``` ::: ::: **Spectral Clustering with Fiedler Vector** The Fiedler vector (the eigenvector for the second-smallest eigenvalue) naturally splits a graph into two clusters based on the sign of each entry -- nodes with the same sign belong to the same community: ::: {#fb5c1208 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Two-way spectral clustering g = ec.Graph(directed=False) # Create graph with two communities... for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") # Dense intra-community edges g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") # Sparse inter-community edge g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=3) fiedler_vector = spec['vectors'][1] # Second eigenvector (λ₂) # Entry j of the vector belongs to node spec['nodes'][j] labels = [g.get_label_from_id(node_id) for node_id in spec['nodes']] # Partition based on sign of Fiedler vector cluster_1 = [lab for lab, v in zip(labels, fiedler_vector) if v < 0] cluster_2 = [lab for lab, v in zip(labels, fiedler_vector) if v >= 0] # Returns the two clusters found via the Fiedler vector cluster_1, cluster_2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (['n3', 'n4', 'n5'], ['n0', 'n1', 'n2']) ``` ::: ::: **Measuring Graph Expansion** The algebraic connectivity (`λ₂`) bounds how well-connected a graph is: a large value indicates an expander graph that's hard to partition, while a small value signals a bottleneck that's easy to cut: ::: {#fce91a1d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") # Algebraic connectivity measures expansion spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=2) # Cheeger inequality: h²/(2Δ) ≤ λ₂ ≤ 2h # where h = edge expansion, Δ = max degree # A small value here reflects the sparse bridge between the two dense halves spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 0.2679491924311226 ``` ::: ::: **Normalized Laplacian for Weighted Graphs** Normalizing the Laplacian accounts for degree variations and constrains eigenvalues to the range `[0, 2]`, which is useful when edge weights differ substantially: ::: {#23a49107 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="B", target="C", weight=2.0) g.add_edge(source="C", target="A", weight=0.5) # Normalized Laplacian accounts for degree variations spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="all", normalized=True) # Eigenvalues in [0, 2] for undirected graphs # λ = 0 ⟺ connected component, λ = 2 ⟺ bipartite structure spec['values'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` [2.2204460492503136e-16, 1.2312580750567148, 1.7687419249432845] ``` ::: ::: **Random Walk and Diffusion Analysis** The algebraic connectivity also governs how fast a random walk mixes on the graph -- larger values mean the walk converges to its steady state more quickly: ::: {#57aefeea .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) for i in range(6): g.add_node(label=f"n{i}") g.add_edge(source="n0", target="n1") g.add_edge(source="n1", target="n2") g.add_edge(source="n3", target="n4") g.add_edge(source="n4", target="n5") g.add_edge(source="n2", target="n3") # Laplacian eigenvalues determine diffusion speed spec = g.get_laplacian_spectrum(which="smallest", k=5) # Mixing time ≈ 1 / λ₂ (algebraic connectivity) # Small λ₂ -> slow mixing, large λ₂ -> fast mixing spec['algebraic_connectivity'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 0.2679491924311226 ``` ::: :::
